q-80631.name: Question 1
q-80631.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ are bases of ${R}^{3}$ and ${R}^{2}$, respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$
q-80631.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-2{b}_{3})+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}(5{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2{x}_{1}){b}_{3}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+(5{x}_{3}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}(3{b}_{1})+\frac{{x}_{2}}{5}(5{b}_{2})+(-\frac{{x}_{3}}{2})(-2{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-94866.name: Question 2
q-94866.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
q-94866.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that

$$
1\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-matrix is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 12 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]=0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-94867.name: Question 3
q-94867.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
q-94867.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+c\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & c \\ 0 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation x1⋅[1000]+x2⋅[0001]+x3⋅[0100]=[0000] is true if and only if x1=x2=x3=0. So, the set is linearly independent.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, [230−4]=2⋅[1000]+(−4)⋅[0001]+3⋅[0100].

  • Statement III is false. For example, the matrix [1111] can't be written as a linear combination of {[1000],[0001],[0100]} since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry a21=0: a⋅[1000]+b⋅[0001]+c⋅[0100]=[ac0b]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-94942.name: Question 4
q-94942.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},w}$ is linearly independent
- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent
- ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}$ is a basis of $V$
q-94942.worked_solution:
Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent.

- Statement II is false. Since if ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{2})+{x}_{3}(2{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{2}+(2{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${{b}_{1},3{b}_{2},2{b}_{3}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+\frac{{x}_{2}}{3}(3{b}_{2})+\frac{{x}_{3}}{2}(2{b}_{3})
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."
